toc.title: Specialized stores, migration, idle databases and practice

html:
1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. RDS: Relational Database Service; DAX: DynamoDB Accelerator; AZ: Availability Zone; IA: Infrequent Access; RI: Reserved Instance; DMS: Database Migration Service

  • Choose the cheapest database type and engine for a workload
  • Plan capacity: instance size, capacity units, serverless options
  • Use caching, read replicas and connection proxies to avoid bigger databases
  • Set backup and retention policies that control storage cost
  • Pick columnar and time series stores, and plan migrations between engines

2Engines, capacity and pricing options

Running case

Lantern and Loom Trims the Database Bill

  • The orders table has unpredictable traffic
  • The Aurora cluster is I/O heavy and costs more every month
  • Lambda functions open too many connections
  • Sensor readings from the warehouse pile up
  • Snapshots from years ago are still billing: cut the bill, keep recovery

Choosing a Cost-Effective Database

Need Cost-effective choice
Key-value at any scale, pay per use DynamoDB
Relational, joins, transactions RDS or Aurora
Analytics over huge tables Redshift (columnar)
Time series such as sensors Timestream
Cassandra-compatible wide column Keyspaces
Hot reads ElastiCache or DAX in front
  • Open-source engines (MySQL, PostgreSQL) avoid commercial license fees
  • Relational is not always cheaper: do not force non-relational data into it
Exam tip

Pick the engine that fits the access pattern, then the cheapest way to run it.

Capacity Planning

Database What you size and pay for
RDS Instance class, storage (gp3), Multi-AZ; storage autoscaling
Aurora Instances plus storage that grows automatically; replicas
Aurora Serverless v2 Aurora capacity units (ACUs) that scale with load
DynamoDB Read and write capacity units or pay per request
Redshift Node type and count, or serverless capacity
  • Measure first, then size: over-provisioning is the commonest waste
  • Compute Optimizer reviews RDS, Aurora and DynamoDB utilization
Exam tip

Unknown or spiky load points to serverless or on-demand; steady load points to provisioned plus a commitment.

DynamoDB Capacity Modes and Table Classes

Option How it bills Use it when
On-demand Per request Unpredictable or new traffic, no planning
Provisioned Capacity you set, per hour Steady, forecastable traffic
Provisioned + auto scaling Follows target utilization Daily curves you can bound
Reserved capacity 1 or 3 year commitment on provisioned Steady baseline
Standard-IA table class Lower storage, higher request cost Storage is the main cost
  • Switching between the two capacity modes is allowed with limits
Exam tip

Spiky or unknown traffic: on-demand. Steady and predictable: provisioned.

Aurora Cost Options [Verify live]

Option How it bills Use it when
Aurora Standard Instances + storage + per-I/O charges Low to moderate I/O
Aurora I/O-Optimized No I/O charges, higher instance and storage I/O above about 25% of Aurora spend
Serverless v2 ACUs per second; scales up and down Variable or spiky load
Provisioned instances Per instance hour Steady load, with RIs
  • I/O-Optimized applies to the whole cluster; switch once every 30 days
  • Serverless v2 can scale to zero and pause when idle. As of 5 November 2026, check the minimum capacity setting
Exam tip

I/O charges are a large share of the Aurora bill: choose I/O-Optimized.

Database Savings Plans and Reserved Instances [Verify live]

Commitment Covers Notes
Database Savings Plans Aurora, RDS, DynamoDB, ElastiCache and other database services $ per hour, 1 year; up to 35%, with lower savings on provisioned
Reserved Instances RDS, Aurora, ElastiCache, Redshift nodes A specific engine and class
DynamoDB reserved capacity Provisioned capacity Steady baseline only
  • As of 5 November 2026, Database Savings Plans follow you across engines, sizes and Regions
  • A workload gets one discount: plans and RIs do not stack
Exam tip

Steady database baseline: commit. Check current coverage and discounts before you rely on them.

Caching, Read Replicas and Connection Pooling

Tool What it saves
ElastiCache Serves hot reads from memory, so the database can be smaller
DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) In-memory cache for DynamoDB reads at microsecond latency
Read replicas Offload reads; cheaper than a larger primary when reads dominate
RDS Proxy Pools connections, so Lambda or bursty apps need smaller instances
  • Cache-aside: check the cache, then the database, then fill the cache
  • Replicas add instance and storage cost: add them only for read pressure
Exam tip

Read-heavy, repeated queries: cache first. Many short connections: RDS Proxy.

Backup and Retention Policies

  • RDS automated backups: retention 0 to 35 days; free backup storage equals 100% of provisioned storage in a Region
  • Manual snapshots stay until deleted, so delete the unneeded
  • Snapshots are incremental; cross-Region copies add storage and transfer cost
  • DynamoDB: point-in-time recovery up to 35 days, plus on-demand backups
  • AWS Backup lifecycle moves copies to cold storage and expires them

Exam tip

Shortest retention that meets the recovery goal, and delete manual snapshots you no longer need.

3Specialized stores, migration, idle databases and practice

Columnar and Time Series Stores

Store Format Cost levers
Amazon Redshift Columnar warehouse RA3 separates compute from storage; pause and resume; serverless for light use; RIs for steady use
Amazon Timestream Time series Memory and magnetic tiers with retention; no servers
Amazon Keyspaces Wide column (Cassandra) On-demand or provisioned capacity
S3 + Athena Query in place Pay per query; best for ad hoc analysis
  • Pausing stops compute billing but storage still bills
Exam tip

Occasional analytics: serverless or Athena. Steady 24-hour warehouse: provisioned with reserved nodes.

Choosing Engines and Migrating

Migration Tool Note
Homogeneous (same engine) DMS Often a lift and shift; continuous replication possible
Heterogeneous (different engine) DMS Schema Conversion plus DMS Convert schema and code first, then move data
Commercial to open source Move to Aurora or open-source RDS Removes license fees
  • DMS bills for the replication instance (or serverless) by the hour: stop it when done
  • Choose the engine for features and skills first, then license and run cost
  • MySQL vs PostgreSQL: pick by application support, not price
Exam tip

Cheaper database through a different engine: heterogeneous migration with schema conversion and DMS.

Stop Idle and Non-Production Databases

Technique Effect
Stop an RDS or Aurora instance No instance charge; storage still bills; restarts automatically after 7 days
Single-AZ for dev and test Avoids the second instance
Serverless v2 for dev Scales down when idle
Smaller classes off hours Fewer ACUs or node hours
Delete unused snapshots and idle replicas Removes ongoing storage and instance cost
  • Keep Multi-AZ and replicas for production only
  • Cost allocation tags on databases; Cost Explorer, Budgets and the Cost and Usage Report show spend; consolidated billing shares discounts
Exam tip

Test databases idle at night: stop them or use serverless, not Multi-AZ.

Choosing the Cheapest Database

  • Key-value, unknown traffic: DynamoDB on-demand
  • Key-value, steady: DynamoDB provisioned with auto scaling
  • Relational, variable: Aurora Serverless v2
  • Relational, steady: RDS or Aurora with a commitment
  • Analytics: Redshift or Athena; sensors: Timestream

Exam tip

Name the data model and the traffic shape, then pick the cheapest capacity model.

What the Exam Asks: Cost-Optimized Databases

  • Which database type fits the data and cost
  • Which capacity mode: on-demand, provisioned or serverless
  • Which commitment: Database Savings Plans, RIs or reserved capacity
  • Which backup and retention policy controls storage cost
  • Which migration tool moves the data between engines
Exam tip

Look for the clues: unpredictable, steady, I/O heavy, sensors, idle, license.

Design Check: Lantern and Loom Trims the Database Bill

Requirement Design
Unpredictable orders traffic DynamoDB on-demand
I/O-heavy Aurora cluster Aurora I/O-Optimized
Lambda connection storms RDS Proxy
Sensor readings Timestream with retention
Old snapshots still billing Delete them; shorten retention
Steady relational baseline Database Savings Plan or RIs
Idle test databases Stop or serverless
  • Cover the right column, answer each row yourself, then compare

4Exam Q&A

4.1 Practice questions (choose the best answer; some ask for two)

S1The Lantern and Loom orders table has unpredictable traffic, with long quiet periods and sudden bursts. The team does not want to plan capacity or pay for unused throughput. Which option fits?

  • ADynamoDB provisioned mode with a fixed high capacity
  • BDynamoDB on-demand capacity mode
  • CA large RDS instance with Multi-AZ
  • DReserved DynamoDB capacity for three years
Show the answer

Answer: B. On-demand mode bills per request with no capacity planning, which suits unpredictable traffic. Fixed or reserved capacity pays for unused throughput during quiet periods, and a large Multi-AZ instance adds cost.

S2A steady Aurora cluster at Lantern and Loom pays a large per-I/O charge that is more than 25% of its Aurora bill. The workload is stable. What should the architect do to cut cost?

  • ASwitch the cluster to Aurora I/O-Optimized
  • BSwitch the cluster to Aurora Standard
  • CAdd more read replicas
  • DMove to a larger instance class
Show the answer

Answer: A. Aurora I/O-Optimized removes per-I/O charges in exchange for higher instance and storage prices, and pays off when I/O is a large share of spend. Standard keeps the I/O charges, and replicas or larger instances add cost.

S3Which TWO actions reduce database backup cost while still meeting the recovery goal? (Select TWO.)

  • ACopy every snapshot to three other Regions
  • BSet backup retention to the maximum for every database
  • CSet automated backup retention to the shortest period that meets the recovery goal
  • DKeep every manual snapshot forever
  • EDelete manual snapshots that are no longer needed
Show the answer

Answer: C, E. Backup storage grows with retention and with copies, so keep automated backups only as long as the recovery goal needs, and delete manual snapshots that are no longer needed. Extra Region copies, maximum retention and keeping every snapshot all add cost.

S4Warehouse sensors send readings every few seconds, and queries ask for trends over time windows. The team wants a serverless store built for this data, with older data moved to cheaper storage. Which service fits?

  • AAmazon RDS for MySQL with a large instance
  • BAmazon Redshift with a provisioned cluster
  • CAmazon Neptune
  • DAmazon Timestream
Show the answer

Answer: D. Timestream is a serverless time series database with memory and magnetic tiers and retention settings that move older data to cheaper storage. RDS and Redshift need capacity planning, and Neptune is a graph database.

S5Hundreds of Lambda functions open database connections at Lantern and Loom, which forces the team to run a much larger RDS instance than the queries need. How can they reduce cost?

  • AAdd a second Availability Zone to the RDS instance
  • BIncrease the connection limit and keep the larger instance
  • CPlace RDS Proxy in front of the database
  • DCreate a read replica in another Region
Show the answer

Answer: C. RDS Proxy pools and shares connections, so the database can be smaller. A second zone, a bigger limit or a cross-Region replica adds cost and does not remove the connection pressure.

5Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Pick the type DynamoDB, RDS, Aurora, Redshift, Timestream by access pattern
Pick the capacity model on-demand or serverless for spiky; provisioned plus commitment for steady
Avoid bigger databases cache, read replicas, RDS Proxy
Control copies shortest retention, delete manual snapshots
Migrate DMS, with schema conversion for a new engine
